title: Tiddalik the Frog
text:
In a story from the Gunai (Kurnai) people of Gippsland in southeastern Australia, there was once a giant frog called Tiddalik. One morning he woke up with an enormous thirst, and he began to drink. He drank the creeks, the billabongs and the rivers until there was no water left anywhere. His belly swelled like a hill, and all the other animals and plants began to die of thirst.

The animals met to decide what to do. Someone had the idea that if Tiddalik could be made to laugh, the water would spill out of him. So one after another they tried. The kookaburra told his funniest stories. Other animals pulled faces, danced and played tricks. Tiddalik only sat there, swollen and sulky, staring at them.

At last Nabunum the eel, who had come out of the dry mud, began to dance. He twisted and turned, wriggled himself into knots and untied them again. Tiddalik's mouth began to twitch. Then he burst out laughing, and as he laughed, the water poured out of him and filled the rivers and lakes again.
lesson: When one person holds what everyone needs, force may not work. A group that keeps trying different approaches, with patience and good humor, can still find the one that does.
people: Tiddalik, the animals, Nabunum the eel
source: Australian Aboriginal oral tradition of the Gunai (Kurnai) people
caveat: Widely known versions are modern retellings, and the animals involved vary.
